opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a real tension here. When a lab releases a model, there's this expectation that you'll put out a big table: here's our number on this benchmark, here's the competitor's number, and we're bolded in most of the columns. Everyone does it because everyone else does it, and if you don't, people assume you're hiding something. That's what makes it an equilibrium. No single lab can unilaterally stop without looking bad.

The problem is what it does to incentives. Once those grids become the scoreboard, there's enormous pressure to optimize for the specific benchmarks that go in the table, whether or not that's what makes the model more useful or more capable in a general sense. You get subtle overfitting. Sometimes it's not even intentional. Benchmark data leaks into training sets, or you make lots of small decisions that happen to favor the evals you know you'll be judged on. Then the numbers drift away from what people actually experience when they use the model.

There's also a comparability problem. Different labs run evals with different prompting, different numbers of samples, different amounts of test-time compute. Two numbers sitting next to each other in a grid look comparable, but often they aren't. Especially now that models can think for a long time, a score without the compute budget attached is kind of meaningless. You can almost always buy a few more points by letting the model think longer or sample more.

And benchmarks saturate really quickly now. Something that was supposed to be hard for years gets to 90% in a few months. So the grid keeps rotating to new benchmarks, and the field spends a lot of energy on that churn instead of on understanding what the models can and can't do.

I'm not saying evals are bad. We need good measurement. But I'd rather see more emphasis on held-out, harder-to-game evaluations, on transparency about how numbers were produced, and honestly on real-world usage. Ultimately, whether people find the model valuable for their actual problems is the evaluation that matters most, and a grid of bolded numbers is a pretty lossy proxy for that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says labs are expected to publish benchmark tables and that everyone does so because everyone else does, sustaining the equilibrium.

r002.rationale: The candidate criticizes grids and suggests alternative evaluation practices, but does not propose publicly acknowledging the equilibrium to make companies comfortable omitting grids from future release headlines.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that bothers me about the eval grids is that they've become the product in a way they were never meant to be. Originally a benchmark was a tool for the researcher. You had a hypothesis, you ran the eval, the number told you whether the idea worked. It was internal diagnostic information. Now the grid is the first thing in the release post, and that changes the incentive for everybody involved.

Once you know a specific set of numbers is going to be the headline, you start optimizing for those numbers, consciously or not. You pick the evals that favor your approach. You tune the prompting, the number of samples, the scaffolding, until the comparison looks good. And every lab is doing the same thing, so you end up with a table where the methodology is subtly different in every cell and nobody can actually tell what's being measured. The numbers go up, the benchmarks saturate, and the public takes away a signal that doesn't correspond to how much more useful the model actually is.

That's why I call it a bad equilibrium rather than just a bad practice. No single lab can unilaterally stop. If you publish fewer numbers, people assume you're hiding something. If you publish honest numbers with conservative settings, you look worse than the lab next door that squeezed every point out. So everyone keeps playing, and the information content of the whole exercise keeps going down.

What I'd rather see is a shift toward things that are harder to game. Evaluations held out by third parties, tasks that are closer to real work, and honestly just people using the models. In the end that's the eval that matters. Did it do the thing you needed? The grid is a very lossy proxy for that, and I think we've gotten a little too attached to it.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation grids have become the first item in release posts, that every lab keeps publishing them, and that publishing fewer numbers makes others assume a lab is hiding something. This communicates how routine publication sustains the expectation.

r002.rationale: The response calls the situation a bad equilibrium and suggests harder-to-game evaluations, but does not propose publicly acknowledging the equilibrium to make companies comfortable omitting grids from future release headlines.

astra-6.text:
I think evaluations are useful. The bad equilibrium is when a grid of benchmark scores becomes the main thing every lab competes on. Once you publish a benchmark and everyone knows that’s how they’ll be judged, there’s a huge incentive to optimize for it. And that can mean improving the underlying capability, but it can also mean making choices that improve the score without making the model much more useful.

Then it’s hard for any one lab to step away. If everybody else has a table full of green cells and you don’t, people assume your model is worse. So everyone keeps playing the same game, even if the differences in that table don’t tell users very much about which model will actually help them.

What I’d rather see is more emphasis on whether a model can accomplish something meaningful: can it solve a difficult problem, can it do a task reliably, can it save somebody time? Those things are harder to compress into a single number, but they’re closer to what we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response says labs publish benchmark tables and compete on them, but does not explain that routine publication with model releases sustains an expectation that each release include an evaluation grid.

r002.rationale: It describes the equilibrium as bad and favors task-focused evaluation, but does not propose publicly acknowledging the problem to make companies comfortable leaving grids out of future release headlines.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the problem is that once you publish a grid comparing your model to everyone else’s, there’s a lot of pressure to make sure your model wins. And there are so many choices that go into an evaluation—which benchmarks you include, how you prompt the models, how much compute you give them—that you can get a pretty flattering picture without any individual number being false.

Then, if everyone else is doing that and you publish a more conservative comparison, your model looks worse. So even people who would prefer a more rigorous process have an incentive to participate. That’s the bad equilibrium.

I’d much rather see evaluations coming from independent parties, and users testing models on the tasks they actually care about. A single grid makes it look like there’s one universally best model, when the answer depends a lot on what you’re trying to do and what resources you’re willing to spend.

r001.rationale: The response describes pressure to publish grids and says “everyone else is doing that,” but does not explain that companies’ routine publication of grids sustains an expectation that releases include them.

r002.rationale: The response calls the equilibrium bad and prefers independent evaluations, but does not propose publicly acknowledging it to make companies comfortable omitting grids from future release headlines.
